decks.name: U19 Grammar · Reported speech
decks.desc: Unit 19: Reported speech. When you report what someone said, the verb usually moves one step back into the past: present simple - past simple; present continuous - past continuous; will - would; can - could. 'I like jazz,' said Ben. - 'Ben said (that) he liked jazz.' The word that is optional. decks.name: U10 Grammar · Conditional sentences

decks.name: U11 Grammar · Past perfect
decks.desc: Unit 11: Past perfect. Past perfect = had + past participle, the same for all persons: I had left. She hadn't eaten. Had they arrived? Use it for an action that happened before another action or time in the past: When we got to the station, the train had gone. The later action is in the past simple; the earlier one is in the past perfect: I was hungry because I hadn't had breakfast.

She was tired because she ____ (not / sleep) well. | hadn't slept
Past perfect = ____ + past participle. (had / have / was) | had

decks.name: U12 Vocabulary · Travel; Phrases with on
decks.desc: Unit 12: Travel; Phrases with on. Word | simple definition.

decks.name: U12 Grammar · Modals: obligation, necessity and advice (2)
decks.desc: Unit 12: Modals: obligation, necessity and advice (2). Should / shouldn't + infinitive gives advice: You should pack a jumper. You shouldn't carry too much cash. Need to + infinitive means it is important or necessary: You need to book early in summer. Have to + infinitive means it is necessary because of a rule or law: You have to wear a seat belt.

Correct it: He don't need to come. | He doesn't need to come.
You look lost. You ____ ask someone for directions. (should / needn't) | should

decks.name: U13 Vocabulary · Social media; Phrases with in

like | to click a button showing you enjoy a photo or message

in future | from now on
in general | usually, in most cases
in particular | especially; more than others

decks.name: U13 Grammar · The passive
decks.desc: Unit 13: The passive. Passive = the verb be + past participle. Change be to show the tense. Present simple passive: am/is/are + past participle: These phones are made in Korea. Past simple passive: was/were + past participle: The bridge was built in 1890. With modal verbs use modal + be + past participle: Helmets must be worn. It can be done.

My bike ____ (steal) last night. | was stolen

Correct it: The rooms is cleaned daily. | The rooms are cleaned daily.
This problem can ____ (solve) easily. | be solved
____ the photos taken by your sister? (Were / Did / Was) | Were

decks.name: U14 Vocabulary · Verbs for cooking
decks.desc: Unit 14: Verbs for cooking. Word | simple definition.
words: bake | to cook bread or cakes in an oven

decks.name: U14 Grammar · Relative clauses
decks.desc: Unit 14: Relative clauses. Defining relative clauses say which person or thing we mean. They have no commas: The boy who sits next to me is Italian. Use who for people, which for things, that for people or things, whose for possession and where for places. In defining clauses you can leave out who, which or that when it is the object: The film (that) we saw was great. You cannot leave it out when it is the subject.

Can we leave out 'who'? 'The man who called was angry.' (yes / no) | no

decks.name: U15 Vocabulary · Artificial and natural world; Phrasal verbs
decks.desc: Unit 15: Artificial and natural world; Phrasal verbs. Word | simple definition.

decks.name: U15 Grammar · Articles: a/an, the and zero article
decks.desc: Unit 15: Articles: a/an, the and zero article. Use a/an with a singular countable noun when you mention it for the first time or say someone's job: I saw a fox. She's an engineer. Use the when you mention something again, when there is only one, or when it is clear which one you mean: The fox ran away. The moon is bright. Use the with superlatives and with seas, rivers, mountain ranges and plural country names: the best, the Atlantic, the Alps, the Netherlands.

decks.name: U16 Grammar · Reported speech
decks.desc: Unit 16: Reported speech. When the reporting verb is past (said, told), the tense usually moves back: present simple to past simple, present continuous to past continuous, past simple and present perfect to past perfect, will to would, can to could. Could, would, should and might do not change. Pronouns and possessives often change: 'I like my job' - She said she liked her job.

'I work in a bank.' She said she ____ in a bank. | worked

decks.name: U17 Vocabulary · Verbs of communication

decks.name: U17 Grammar · Reported questions
decks.desc: Unit 17: Reported questions. Reported questions use statement word order (subject before verb) and no question mark: 'Where is the bank?' - He asked where the bank was. Tenses move back as in reported statements: 'What are you doing?' - She asked what I was doing. Do, does and did disappear: 'Where do you live?' - She asked where I lived. For yes/no questions use if or whether: 'Are you ready?' - She asked if I was ready.

'Will you come?' She asked if I ____ come. | would

decks.name: U18 Grammar · have something done
decks.desc: Unit 18: have something done. Form: have + object + past participle: I have my eyes tested every year. Use it when another person, usually a professional, does a job for you: We had the car repaired (= a mechanic repaired it). Compare: I cut my hair (I did it myself) and I had my hair cut (someone else did it).

decks.name: U19 Grammar · Different types of clause
decks.desc: Unit 19: Different types of clause. Contrast: although, whereas and while join two ideas that are different or surprising: Although it was cold, we swam. Although and whereas can go at the start or in the middle; while (for contrast) usually starts the sentence: While I like the city, I wouldn't live there.

decks.name: U20 Grammar · Verbs with two objects
decks.desc: Unit 20: Verbs with two objects. Some verbs can have two objects: a direct object (usually a thing) and an indirect object (usually a person): Dad gave me a watch. Pattern 1: verb + person + thing, with no preposition: She sent her friend a postcard. Pattern 2: verb + thing + to/for + person: She sent a postcard to her friend.

decks.name: U2 Grammar · Present tense review

decks.name: U3 Grammar · Past tense review
